column4: The section describes an opening name as a raised identifying sign; this ayah says Solomon’s letter is “from Solomon” and begins with “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful,” using the divine name to mark the message’s source.
The section’s herd is separated for sacrifice and brought to its destination; this ayah says the offering must reach its place (مَحِلَّهُ), within the completion of pilgrimage for God.
The section joins approval and wrath to the account day; this ayah directly contrasts following God’s pleasure (رِضْوَانَ اللَّهِ) with incurring His anger (سَخَطٍ), whose destination is Hell.

The section distinguishes a sign or name from what it points to; Joseph says the gods worshipped besides Allah are only names people have named, with no authority, then says judgment belongs to God alone and commands worship of Him.
The section’s weary servant asks his Lord for help; this ayah commands people to seek help (اسْتَعِينُوا) through patience and prayer, a direct use of the same help-root as the section’s “nastaʿīn.”

The section contrasts falling under wrath with finding the way; this ayah says whoever follows God’s guidance will neither go astray (يَضِلُّ) nor be wretched, making guidance the stated boundary against loss.

The section’s lost-way image meets the wording “He found you lost and guided you” (ضَالًّا فَهَدَى); the verse does not stage a lost traveler, so this is a specific lexical parallel whose precise sense is uncertain.

The section links a lapse of memory with disappearance from the way; during Moses’s journey, his companion says he forgot the fish and it took its way into the sea, a concrete but indirect meeting of forgetting and loss.
After the lost fish in 18:63, Moses recognizes it as what they sought and they retrace their tracks; this ayah contributes the return along a path, not the forgetting that began the episode.
This continues the call to seek help in 2:45: the humble are certain they will meet their Lord and return to Him, matching the section’s servant addressing the owner at the end of a journey.

After the riders remember God’s subjection of their mounts in 43:13, this ayah has them say they will return to their Lord, giving the section’s traveler’s road a stated destination beyond the journey.

The section joins the balance to people standing for judgment; this ayah depicts the book set out, prophets and witnesses brought, and judgment made in truth, supplying a concrete scene of the reckoning.
This continues the judgment scene in 39:69: every soul is paid in full for what it did, a specific account-day outcome related to the section’s scales.
